To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Li-Fraumani syndrome is a rare autosomal dominant cancer syndrome that is characterized by early-onset breast cancer in women, sarcomas, brain tumors and other cancers, and that is caused by mutations in the TP53 gene.
the p53 gene is mutated in a subset of LFS families, that the mutation is found in a "hot spot", and that the mutation is a germline event.
germline mutations of p53 have been detected in 2 out of 8 families with Li-Fraumenli syndrome.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and analysis of mutations in the p53 tumor suppressor gene in patients with cancer.
the molecular genetic analysis of inherited cancer susceptibility syndromes.
the identification and characterization of the molecular defects of the p53 tumor suppressor gene in Li-Fraumani syndrome (LFS) families.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
p53 mutation is the genetic lesion in a subset of families with LFS and that this subset is not yet defined.
germline p53 mutations are not found in all families with LFs, but are found in a subset of families with this syndrome.
germline p53 mutations are not a prerequisite for Li-Fraumenie syndrome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is no simple relationship between the presence of germline p53 mutations and the Li-Fraumani syndrome.

the presence of a p53 mutation in a family with LFS should be regarded as a "strong" indicator that other members of the family are at increased risk of developing cancer, but that the presence of such a mutation in a family should not automatically be taken as an indicator of the presence of LFS.
p53 mutations are not the primary cause of LFS, but rather a secondary event.
The main takeaway from our work is that
p53 mutation testing should not be used to determine eligibility for clinical trials.
p53 mutations in LFS are not always germline.
the presence of a p53 mutation in an affected family member does not exclude the possibility of a de novo mutation in an unaffected family member.
